kurals.tamil:
இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்
குன்ற வருப விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Indri amaiyaach chirappina aayinum
Kundra varupa vidal.
kurals.meaning: Even if certain acts are so important that life seems impossible without them, give them up if doing them would lower your dignity and the honour of your family.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you could win the biggest prize at school, but only by copying someone else's answers. The prize feels like something you cannot live without, but this kural says: if getting it makes you smaller inside, walk away from it.
kurals.university: The chapter on maanam (மானம், honour, self-respect) follows Kudimai (Nobility of Family) and is read in the Parimelazhagar tradition as the quality of never sinking below one's station. The opening couplet sets the bar at its highest: indri amaiyaa (இன்றி அமையா, 'that without which one cannot exist') describes acts that seem indispensable, and kundra varupa (குன்ற வருப) are acts that bring about a 'lowering' (kundru, to diminish), which must be let go (vidal, விடல்). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan both gloss the lowering as a fall in kudi-p-perumai (the honour of one's lineage), tying the chapter to the preceding one; Kalaignar generalises it to one's own dignity. The Pope translation quoted on ytamizh.com renders it 'Reject each act that may thine honour's clearness stain.' The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Bharata returns to Ayodhya and learns that his mother Kaikeyi has won him the throne by having Rama exiled, he refuses the kingdom, rebukes her, and goes to the forest to beg Rama to return, later ruling only as Rama's regent with Rama's sandals on the throne.
hinduism.explanation: Bharata is offered the greatest prize a prince can have, but because it came through a shameful scheme, he will not take it.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's case: something of the highest value is refused because accepting it would stain one's honour and family.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Bharata's refusal of the throne)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit on refusing a great gain obtained dishonourably; paraphrased from the well-known episode, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter; Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;”
christianity.explanation: Moses gives up a royal position and its comforts rather than keep them on terms that would betray who he is.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it praises giving up great advantages when keeping them would cost one's integrity.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good fit on renouncing high position; the motive is faith in God rather than personal or family honour.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Not equal are the evil and the good, although the abundance of evil might impress you.’ So fear Allah, O you of understanding, that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran warns that a large gain from wrong should not tempt a person, because good and evil are never equal however much the evil seems to offer.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that even a great, seemingly necessary gain must be dropped when it comes by a degrading route.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the principle of refusing attractive but wrong gain; does not speak of honour or lineage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Abram said to the king of Sodom: ‘I have lifted up my hand unto the LORD, God Most High, Maker of heaven and earth, that I will not take a thread nor a shoe-latchet nor aught that is thine, lest thou shouldest say: I have made Abram rich;’”
judaism.explanation: After a victory, Abraham refuses the spoils he was entitled to, so that no one could claim to have made him rich.
judaism.tie_back: A near one-to-one match: a lawful and valuable gain is refused because accepting it would diminish his standing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit: Abraham guards his dignity by refusing a gain he could have taken.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises the person who will not do wrong for any gain, even for family, wealth or a kingdom.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that even the greatest goods must not be pursued by a lowering act.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong fit on refusing success by unjust means; frames it as virtue rather than honour.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The tiger of the forest having slain an elk, will not eat it, but will leave it if it fall on the left side. In like manner, could the excellent by a sacrifice of principle obtain all the wealth that exists under the wide-extended heavens, they would not even desire it.”
jainism.explanation: This Jain Tamil quatrain from the Naladiyar's chapter on honour says the noble would not want all the world's wealth if it cost them their principles.
jainism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural's own claim: even what seems indispensable is refused when it would lower one's honour.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 30 (மானம், 'Honour'; titled 'Innocence' in this translation), stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Tamil Jain text from the Naladiyar's own Maanam chapter, so very close to the Kural; used over canonical scripture because it addresses honour directly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: During Odysseus' twenty-year absence, Penelope is pressed by many suitors to remarry, which would end the strain on her household; she delays them for years with the trick of weaving and unweaving Laertes' shroud rather than give up her loyalty.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope refuses an easy way out of her troubles because it would betray her husband and her house.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's noble person, she gives up relief that seems necessary because taking it would lower her honour.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 2 and 19 (Penelope and the suitors)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Partial fit: loyalty and household honour rather than refusing an indispensable act.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells his jury that a good person weighs only whether an act is right, not whether it saves his life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural also says that even what seems necessary for survival must be dropped if it is degrading.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong fit on putting right action above even survival; Socrates speaks of justice rather than family honour.

kurals.tamil:
சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யாரே சீரொடு
பேராண்மை வேண்டு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seerinum seeralla seyyaare seerodu
Peraanmai vendu pavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who want both fame and true nobility will not do anything unworthy, even if it would win them fame.
kurals.elementary: Some people will do anything to become famous, even mean or silly things. This kural says that people who want to be both well-known and truly good will never do something shameful just to get noticed.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on seer (சீர், renown, excellence): seerinum (சீரினும், 'even for renown') and seeralla (சீரல்ல, 'what is not excellent', unworthy deeds). Those who desire seerodu peraanmai (சீரொடு பேராண்மை), renown together with great 'manliness' or nobility of spirit, do not do such things. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses peraanmai as பெரிய ஆண்மை and the unworthy acts as those unfit for kudi-p-perumai (family honour); Kalaignar reads it as a heroic life that will not chase fame by acts contrary to self-respect. The point sharpens the previous kural: not only necessity but even fame itself cannot justify a lowering act. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad, Yama teaches Nachiketas that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both come to a person; the wise examine them and choose the good, while the foolish choose the pleasant and miss the true goal.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad separates what is truly good from what merely looks attractive, and praises choosing the good.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's noble person likewise refuses an attractive gain (fame) when it requires an unworthy act.
hinduism._accuracy_note: General principle of choosing the good over the attractive; not specifically about fame or honour.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me. Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan”
christianity.explanation: Jesus is offered all the glory of the world on condition of one unworthy act, and refuses.
christianity.tie_back: A vivid case of the Kural's rule: glory is not worth an act that lowers one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (glory offered for a degrading act, refused); the frame is worship of God rather than personal honour.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever desires honor [through power] - then to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends good speech, and righteous work raises it. But they who plot evil deeds will have a severe punishment, and the plotting of those - it will perish.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says true honour comes only through good speech and righteous work, while evil schemes come to nothing.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it teaches that real honour cannot be reached by unworthy means.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit on honour gained only by righteous means; grounded in God rather than human nobility.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, And loving favour rather than silver and gold.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs ranks a good name above wealth.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural adds that a good name joined to nobility is not to be bought even with fame won unworthily.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shared value of a good name over gain; Proverbs contrasts name with riches, the Kural contrasts true honour with cheap fame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Gains, Offerings, Fame, & Status wrongly gained, and whoever would praise self & disparage others. That, Namuci, is your army, the Dark One's commando force.”
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta names fame and status gained wrongly as part of Mara's army that he must defeat.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too treats fame won by unworthy deeds as something the noble refuse.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 3.2, Padhana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; accesstoinsight.org)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on rejecting wrongly gained fame; the Buddhist goal is liberation, not worldly honour.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The excellent will not do the things which will bring upon them the effects of sin in another birth, or disgrace in this birth, though it should cost them their lives.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain quatrain says the noble avoid any act that brings sin in the next life or disgrace in this one, whatever the cost.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that the honourable will not do unworthy deeds even for renown.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 30 (மானம், 'Honour'), stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Tamil Jain text from the Naladiyar's Maanam chapter; it adds the Jain concern with karmic consequence in a future birth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus' fable, the young Heracles meets two women at a crossroads: Vice offers him an easy, pleasant road, while Virtue offers a hard road of toil that leads to true and lasting glory; he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles chooses the road where glory is earned honestly over an easier road of pleasure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's seekers of renown with nobility, he wants glory only on worthy terms.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus' Choice of Heracles, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit on glory through virtue; the contrast is pleasure versus toil rather than fame versus dishonour.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says that if he can gain wealth while keeping himself modest, faithful and high-minded, he will; but if he must give up his own proper good so that others can gain what is not truly good, it is unjust and foolish to ask it.
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus will accept outward gains only if they leave his character intact.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural applies the same test to fame: it is welcome only if no unworthy act is needed to get it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual fit; paraphrased, and it speaks of wealth and office rather than fame.

kurals.tamil:
பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல் சிறிய
சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Perukkaththu vendum panidhal siriya
Surukkaththu vendum uyarvu.
kurals.meaning: When fortune swells, be humble; when it shrinks to little, hold your head high.
kurals.elementary: When you win a game, it is good to be kind and not show off. When you lose, it is good to stand tall and not beg or sulk. This kural says to bow a little in good times and stand straight in hard times.
kurals.university: A perfectly balanced antithesis: perukkam (பெருக்கம், increase, prosperity) is set against surukkam (சுருக்கம், contraction, want), and panidhal (பணிதல், bending, humility) against uyarvu (உயர்வு, height, unbending dignity). Siriya (சிறிய, 'small') intensifies the second half: in a narrow, reduced state. Mu. Varadarasanar reads uyarvu as 'height that does not bow' (பணியாத உயர்வு), and Solomon Pappaiah as not stooping to others in poverty. Maanam here is not pride but a discipline that runs against circumstance: humble when one could afford arrogance, upright when one is tempted to grovel. Pope's version on ytamizh.com: 'Bow down thy soul, with increase blest, in happy hour; / Lift up thy heart, when stript of all by fortune's power.' Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not disturbed in mind even amidst the threefold miseries or elated when there is happiness, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the steady sage, who is neither shaken by misery nor puffed up by happiness.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural asks for the same steadiness in fortune and misfortune, expressed as humility and dignity.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.56 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit on even-mindedness in both states; the Gita stresses inner calm, the Kural outward bearing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he has learned how to live rightly both in plenty and in need.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural gives the rule for each state: humility in plenty, dignity in need.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close structural match on the two states; Paul stresses contentment rather than the specific virtues named.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you. And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful -”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches neither despair in loss nor pride in gain.
islam.tie_back: This matches both halves of the Kural: no arrogance in prosperity, no collapse in poverty.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close two-sided match; the Quran grounds it in God's decree.

judaism.quote_or_event: Moses warns Israel that when they have eaten their fill, built fine houses, and seen their flocks, silver and gold multiply, their hearts may be lifted up and they may forget the LORD who brought them out of Egypt.
judaism.explanation: The Torah warns that prosperity breeds arrogance and forgetfulness.
judaism.tie_back: This supports the first half of the Kural, humility in prosperity, but not the second.
judaism._accuracy_note: Covers only the prosperity half; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The good renounce (attachment for) everything. The virtuous do not prattle with a yearning for pleasures. The wise show no elation or depression when touched by happiness or sorrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The wise are neither elated by good fortune nor cast down by bad.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural turns this evenness into a rule of conduct: humble in plenty, upright in want.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit on equanimity across both states; less about social dignity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Among all those who live in this fertile and wide world, those who give not alms to others, amongst the rich, though exceeding rich, are poor indeed; while those who go not to beg alms of the rich, though they have become exceedingly poor, are indeed illustrious.”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar says a rich man who does not give is truly poor, while a poor man who will not beg from the rich is truly great.
jainism.tie_back: The second half matches the Kural's dignity in want closely; the first half links right conduct in plenty to generosity rather than humility.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 30 (மானம், 'Honour'), stanza 6 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Tamil Jain text; strong on dignity in poverty, partial on the prosperity half.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus tells how the rich king Croesus asked Solon who was the happiest of men, expecting to be named; Solon refused to call any man happy before his end. Later, defeated and on the pyre, Croesus called out Solon's name and was spared by Cyrus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Croesus' pride in prosperity is humbled, and he learns wisdom in defeat.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the cost of lacking the humility in prosperity that the Kural requires.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates the prosperity half by counterexample; legend recorded by a historian rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book 2 of the Consolation, Lady Philosophy reminds Boethius that Fortune turns her wheel by nature, raising the low and casting down the high, so no one should be puffed up by her gifts or crushed by their loss.
philosophy.explanation: Since fortune always turns, neither rising nor falling should change who a person is.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural draws the practical rule: bow when high, stand tall when low.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good fit on reversals of fortune; paraphrased, and focused on detachment more than dignity.

kurals.tamil:
தலையின் இழிந்த மயிரனையர் மாந்தர்
நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thalaiyin izhindha mayiranaiyar maandhar
Nilaiyin izhindhak kadai.
kurals.meaning: People who fall from their honourable position become like hair that has fallen from the head: once valued, now worthless.
kurals.elementary: Hair on your head is combed and cared for. But once a hair falls on the floor, nobody wants it. This kural says a person who drops their good behaviour and self-respect loses the respect others gave them, just like that fallen hair.
kurals.university: The simile works through a single verb, izhi (இழி, to descend, fall, be debased), used twice: hair izhindha from the head (fallen) and people izhindha from their nilai (நிலை, station, standing). On the head, hair is an ornament; once fallen it is swept away. Mu. Varadarasanar reads thalai as both 'head' and 'high place' (தலைமை), so the image doubles as falling from leadership. The Parimelazhagar tradition places this after 963 to show what happens when the discipline of maanam fails. Kalaignar applies it to someone who held a high place in people's hearts. Pope: 'Like hairs from off the head that fall to earth, / When fall'n from high estate are men of noble birth.' Both online texts read இழிந்தக் கடை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Nahusha is raised to the throne of Indra in heaven, but growing arrogant he forces the great sages to carry his palanquin and kicks Agastya; cursed by the sage, he falls from heaven and becomes a serpent on earth.
hinduism.explanation: A man raised to the highest place falls to the lowest because of conduct unworthy of his position.
hinduism.tie_back: Nahusha is the Kural's fallen hair: honoured while he kept his station, cast down when he left it.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, sections 11-17 (the story of Nahusha)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit for a fall from high station through unworthy conduct; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that salt that loses its saltiness is thrown out and walked on.
christianity.tie_back: The same image as the Kural: something valued, once it loses its quality, is discarded underfoot.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close image of loss of worth and being cast out; applied to disciples rather than people of rank.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then We return him to the lowest of the low,”
islam.explanation: After saying that humanity was created in the best form, the Quran warns that a person can be returned to the lowest state, except those who believe and do good.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes a fall from a high to a debased condition.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of fall from high estate; theological framing and no image of contempt.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How art thou fallen from heaven, O day-star, son of the morning! How art thou cut down to the ground, That didst cast lots over the nations!”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah mocks a proud king who once ruled nations and is now brought down to the ground.
judaism.tie_back: It captures the Kural's contrast between the height one held and the low place one falls to.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong image of a fall from the heights; the cause is pride before God, not loss of personal honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, a monk of noble birth and early renown in the Sangha, grows ambitious, asks to lead the order in the Buddha's place, plots against him and splits the community; he ends disgraced.
buddhism.explanation: A respected disciple loses all standing through conduct unworthy of his place.
buddhism.tie_back: He is a Buddhist example of the Kural's fallen hair: honoured while worthy, cast off when he fell.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit; paraphrased from the canonical account.

jainism.quote_or_event: The first lecture of the Uttaradhyayana Sutra compares a disobedient, unruly and talkative pupil to a dog with sore ears that is driven away everywhere, while the well-behaved pupil is honoured.
jainism.explanation: One who abandons proper conduct is pushed away wherever he goes.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's fallen hair and Jainism's driven-off dog both picture a person rejected after falling from right conduct.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; similar image of rejection, but about a pupil's discipline rather than a person of rank.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Bellerophon, once a favoured hero who slew the Chimaera, later becomes hated by the gods and wanders alone over the Aleian plain, eating out his heart and shunning the paths of men.
greek_mythology.explanation: A celebrated hero ends his life as an outcast.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It pictures the Kural's fall from honoured place to worthlessness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fits the fall-from-esteem image; Homer gives no reason for his fall, which later tradition attributes to pride.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says a person must weigh what his own character is worth and not sell it cheaply; he compares the man of principle to the purple thread in a garment, the small bright stripe that gives the rest its beauty, and says he will not be like the common threads.
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus urges people to stay true to the role that marks them out, rather than sink to the level of the rest.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural warns what happens to those who do sink from their station.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Positive counterpart to the Kural's warning; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் குன்றுவ
குன்றி அனைய செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kundrin anaiyaarum kundruvar kundruva
Kundri anaiya seyin.
kurals.meaning: Even people as great as a mountain are brought low if they do something debasing, even something as small as a kunri seed.
kurals.elementary: A big, beautiful glass of milk can be spoiled by one tiny drop of ink. This kural says even a very great person can lose respect by doing one small mean thing.
kurals.university: A celebrated piece of wordplay on the root kundru (குன்று): kundru as noun means 'hill' (kundrin anaiyaar, those like a hill), as verb 'to diminish' (kundruvar, they will be lowered), kundruva are 'diminishing' (debasing) acts, and kundri (குன்றி) is the kunrimani, the small red-and-black seed of Abrus precatorius used as a jeweller's weight. The contrast of hill and seed sets the scale: the smallest dishonour outweighs the largest standing. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read kundri anaiya as 'even a kunrimani's weight'. Pope keeps the botanical sense: 'If meanness, slight as abrus grain, by men be wrought.' Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At Kurukshetra, Yudhishthira, famed for never lying, tells Drona that Ashvatthama is dead, speaking the words the elephant softly so that Drona believes his son has been killed; his chariot, which had always moved a little above the ground, at once sinks to touch the earth.
hinduism.explanation: A single half-truth from a man renowned for truth brings him down from his elevated state.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's mountain brought low by a seed-sized fault.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Drona Parva (the death of Drona)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative fit (a small deceit lowers a great man); paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a small amount of corruption spreads through the whole.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say that a small wrong is enough to spoil something great.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the 'small fault, large effect' idea; Paul is speaking of false teaching in a community.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says that no evil is too small to be counted.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's seed-sized act, even the smallest wrong matters.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the tiny-measure image; about divine reckoning rather than loss of standing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Dead flies make the ointment of the perfumer fetid and putrid; So doth a little folly outweigh wisdom and honour.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet says a small folly spoils a person's wisdom and honour, as dead flies spoil fine perfume.
judaism.tie_back: An almost one-to-one match: a small act outweighs great honour.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one in idea and in the contrast of tiny cause and great honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Think not lightly of evil, saying, ‘It will not come to me.’ Drop by drop is the water pot filled. Likewise, the fool, gathering it little by little, fills himself with evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that small wrongs add up.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts warn against treating a small wrong as harmless.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the warning about small evils; stresses accumulation rather than one act lowering a great person.

jainism.quote_or_event: After renouncing his kingdom, Bahubali stands motionless in meditation for a year, but omniscience does not come because a trace of pride remains: he will not bow to his younger brothers who became monks before him. Only when his sisters Brahmi and Sundari tell him to get down from the elephant of pride does he let it go and attain kevala jnana.
jainism.explanation: Even a hero of great austerity is held back by a small remnant of pride (mana).
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a tiny fault in a mountain-like person is enough to bring him down.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra, Book 1 (Bharata and Bahubali; tr. Helen M. Johnson)
jainism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit on a small fault in a great person; the fault is pride (here the vice, not honour), so the parallel is in structure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In later tradition, Thetis dips the infant Achilles in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel; that one untouched spot is where Paris' arrow later kills the greatest of the Greek warriors.
greek_mythology.explanation: One small weak point brings down the mightiest hero.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural's contrast between a mountain-sized man and a seed-sized flaw.
greek_mythology.source: Statius, Achilleid 1.133-134, 268-270 (the Styx dipping); not in Homer
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Only a structural fit: the heel is a physical weakness, not a moral act.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes shame (aidos) as a kind of fear of disrepute, and says it suits the young; the good man should not need it, because he will not voluntarily do bad actions at all.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the good person avoids every disgraceful act, not just large ones.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural adds the warning that even a small disgraceful act lowers a great person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.9 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Next-best match on shame and disgraceful acts; lacks the small-act-great-fall point.

kurals.tamil:
புகழ்இன்றால் புத்தேள்நாட்டு உய்யாதால் என்மற்று
இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pugazhindraal puththelnaattu uyyaadhaal enmatru
Ikazhvaarpin sendru nilai.
kurals.meaning: Following and fawning on those who despise you brings no fame in this world and no place in heaven; what then is it good for?
kurals.elementary: Some children follow around a bully who laughs at them, hoping to be liked. This kural asks: what do you get from that? Nobody admires it, and it does not make you a better person. Better to keep your self-respect.
kurals.university: The couplet is a rhetorical question built on the two goods of classical Tamil ethics: pugazh (புகழ், fame in this world) and puththel naadu (புத்தேள் நாடு, the land of the gods, i.e. heaven, reward in the next). Ikazhvaar pin sendru nilai (இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை), 'the state of going after those who scorn one', yields neither, hence en matru (என்மற்று), 'what else then?'. Solomon Pappaiah reads it as abandoning honour in order to live by following one's despisers. Kalaignar's gloss pointedly adds 'a heaven that does not exist', a modern rationalist reading; the older commentators take heaven at face value. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: My dear Arjuna, how have these impurities come upon you? They are not at all befitting a man who knows the value of life. They lead not to higher planets but to infamy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that his collapse of spirit is unworthy and leads neither to heaven nor to fame.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's 'not to higher planets but to infamy' matches the Kural's 'no fame, no heaven' almost word for word.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.2 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical twin verdict (asvargyam akirti-karam); the dishonour in the Gita is faint-heartedness, not servility.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.”
christianity.explanation: Paul refuses to live by pleasing people at the cost of his true calling.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise rejects living by currying favour with others.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial fit on refusing to live as a people-pleaser; does not address being scorned.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those who take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek with them honor [through power]? But indeed, honor belongs to Allah entirely.”
islam.explanation: The Quran asks why anyone would look for honour by attaching themselves to people who do not share or respect their faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says honour cannot be found by following those who hold you in contempt.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on seeking honour from the wrong patrons; the frame is religious allegiance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And all the king’s servants, that were in the king’s gate, bowed down, and prostrated themselves before Haman; for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not down, nor prostrated himself before him.”
judaism.explanation: Mordecai alone refuses to bow before the arrogant Haman, though everyone else does.
judaism.tie_back: He embodies the Kural's refusal to bow and follow after those who hold one in contempt.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit on refusing to stoop to a scornful superior; the text gives no explicit reason.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with evil companions; do not seek the fellowship of the vile. Associate with the good friends; seek the fellowship of noble men.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha advises seeking the company of the noble, not the base.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural adds that attaching oneself to those who despise one brings no good at all.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Next-best: about choosing companions, not about servility toward scorners.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Leave off the causes of sin, acquire fame through patience! (A man who acts up to this) will rise to the upper regions after having left this body of clay.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching names the true way to both goods the Kural mentions: fame in this life and a higher world after death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says fawning on scorners wins neither fame nor heaven; the Jain verse says patience and abandoning sin win both.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 3.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Matches the paired goals (fame and upper world) by contrast; does not speak of servility. In Jain terms the 'upper regions' are heavenly births, not final liberation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After Agamemnon publicly dishonours him by taking Briseis, Achilles refuses the embassy's offer of vast gifts, cities and a royal marriage, saying he will not be won over by the man who insulted him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles will not return to serve a king who scorned him, whatever the reward.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He refuses exactly what the Kural condemns: going after those who held one in contempt.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit; Achilles' pride also has a destructive side the Kural does not endorse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says an invitation to a great man's dinner has a price: flattery and attendance at his door. If you will not pay it, do not complain of going without; you keep instead the dignity of not having flattered.
philosophy.explanation: Courting the powerful costs one's self-respect, and Epictetus advises declining the bargain.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural asks what such following gains; Epictetus answers that refusing it keeps something more valuable.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual fit on the cost of fawning; paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
ஒட்டார்பின் சென்றொருவன் வாழ்தலின் அந்நிலையே
கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Ottaarpin sendroruvan vaazhdhalin annilaiye
Kettaan enappadudhal nandru.
kurals.meaning: It is better to be spoken of as ruined, standing firm in one's own condition, than to make a living by trailing after those who do not value you.
kurals.elementary: Imagine choosing between staying poor but proud, or getting treats every day by doing whatever an unkind person tells you. This kural says it is better to lose the treats and keep your self-respect.
kurals.university: Ottaar (ஒட்டார்) are those who do not 'stick' to one: people who do not regard or accept one, or enemies. Living by following them (pin sendru vaazhdhal) is set against being called kettaan (கெட்டான், 'he is ruined', or 'he perished'). The phrase annilaiye (அந்நிலையே), 'in that very state', is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as remaining in one's own condition without stooping, while Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take kettaan more starkly as 'died'. Pope's English, quoted on ytamizh.com, follows the stronger reading: 'Better 'twere said, He's perished! than to gain / The means to live, following in foeman's train.' The couplet expresses a priority of honour over comfort, not an instruction to seek death. Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that for a person of standing, disgrace is worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same in its own way: better to be called ruined than to live in disgrace.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on preferring loss over dishonour; the Gita's context is a warrior's duty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I have used none of these things: neither have I written these things, that it should be so done unto me: for it were better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void.”
christianity.explanation: Paul refuses to live off the financial support of his churches, saying he would rather die than lose the honour of preaching freely.
christianity.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: better to perish than to live dependent in a way that empties one's honour.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on preferring death to dependent living that compromises one's boast; Paul's patrons were not hostile, unlike the Kural's ottaar.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah, unable to move about in the land. An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Quran praises the poor whose dignity is so strong that people mistake them for well-off, because they will not beg.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours those who would rather endure want than live by depending on others.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on dignity in want; it does not speak of following those who despise one.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, He will deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and out of thy hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.”
judaism.explanation: Three young Jews tell the king they will not bow even if it costs them their lives.
judaism.tie_back: They prefer possible death to living by submitting to a power that demands they betray themselves.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the choice of death over submission; the issue is idolatry rather than personal honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do I carry muñja grass? I spit on my life. Death in battle would be better for me than that I, defeated, survive.”
buddhism.explanation: Facing Mara's army, the Bodhisatta says he would rather die fighting than live on in defeat.
buddhism.tie_back: This strikingly echoes the Kural's 'better to be called dead' than to live in surrender.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 3.2, Padhana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; accesstoinsight.org; the site's text has the typo 'woud')
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in form; the 'battle' is inner struggle against Mara, not social honour.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The honourable, though they become through destitution mere bones and skin, will they follow those who are destitute of proper dispositions, to make known their afflictions to them?”
jainism.explanation: The Naladiyar says the honourable, even when wasted by poverty, will not go after unworthy people to plead their troubles.
jainism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own image of refusing to live by following those who do not value one.
jainism.source: Naladiyar, ch. 30 (மானம், 'Honour'), stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
jainism._accuracy_note: Tamil Jain text from the Naladiyar's Maanam chapter; near one-to-one on refusing to follow the unworthy even in extreme want.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Antigone, forbidden by King Creon to bury her brother, does so anyway, telling Creon she knew she must die some day and that if she dies before her time she counts it gain.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antigone chooses death over obeying a command that would dishonour her and her family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She chooses, like the Kural, to be counted lost rather than live by submitting to one who scorns what she holds sacred.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fits the death-over-submission choice; her motive is sacred duty to the dead rather than self-respect.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I thought that I ought not to do anything common or mean in the hour of danger: nor do I now repent of the manner of my defence, and I would rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live.”
philosophy.explanation: Condemned to death, Socrates says he would rather die true to himself than live by pleading in a way unworthy of him.
philosophy.tie_back: A near one-to-one match: better to be called dead than to live by stooping to those who scorn one.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: death preferred to living by unworthy submission before a hostile court.

kurals.tamil:
மருந்தோமற்று ஊன்ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை பெருந்தகைமை
பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Marundhomatru oonombum vaazhkkai perundhagaimai
Peedazhiya vandha idaththu.
kurals.meaning: When one's greatness and dignity are being destroyed, is a life that merely keeps the body going a medicine against death?
kurals.elementary: Everyone grows old one day, no matter what. This kural asks: if you will not live forever anyway, why trade away your good name just to stay comfortable a little longer?
kurals.university: The rhetorical question marundho (மருந்தோ, 'is it a medicine?') implies a medicine against death (saavaamai, deathlessness), as Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both supply. Oon ombum vaazhkkai (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is a life that merely 'nourishes the flesh', set against perundhagaimai (பெருந்தகைமை, nobility) and peedu (பீடு, dignity, greatness), whose destruction is the occasion. The argument is that since death cannot be escaped, saving the body at the cost of honour gains nothing lasting. Kalaignar makes this explicit: there is no medicine for not dying, so do not lower your worth for a better life. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (some editions divide it மருந்தோமற் றூனோம்பும்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who has taken his birth is sure to die, and after death one is sure to take birth again. Therefore, in the unavoidable discharge of your duty, you should not lament.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reminds Arjuna that death is certain for all who are born, so fear of it should not turn him from duty.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same certainty of death to argue that clinging to bodily life at the cost of honour gains nothing.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.27 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong fit on inevitable death as a reason not to compromise; the Gita adds rebirth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that holding on to life at any cost loses what really matters.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly asks what is gained by preserving the body while losing one's worth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good fit on the futility of saving bodily life at the cost of the soul; 'soul' is not the same as honour.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Indeed, the death from which you flee - indeed, it will meet you. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you about what you used to do.’”
islam.explanation: The Quran reminds those who run from death that it will meet them anyway.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says no amount of self-preservation is a medicine against death.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the inevitability of death; it adds judgment rather than honour.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is no man that hath power over the wind to retain the wind; neither hath he power over the day of death; and there is no discharge in war; neither shall wickedness deliver him that is given to it.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet says no one controls the day of death, and wickedness cannot save the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: This supports the Kural's question: dishonourable survival is no defence against death.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches both the inevitability of death and the futility of wrongdoing as escape.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither in the sky nor in mid-ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts, nowhere in the world is there a place where one will not be overcome by death.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says there is nowhere to hide from death.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural concludes from the same fact that honour should not be traded for a little more life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on inevitability of death; draws no conclusion about honour.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As a lion takes hold of an antelope, so Death leads off a man in his last hour; neither mother, nor father, nor brother will, at that time, save a particle (of his life).”
jainism.explanation: The monk Citra warns King Brahmadatta that death takes everyone and no one can save even a fraction of a life.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same truth to show that clinging to the body at the cost of dignity is pointless.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Strong on inevitable death; Jainism draws the lesson of renunciation and karma, not social honour.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Sarpedon tells Glaucus that if they could escape old age and death by avoiding battle he would not fight; but since countless fates of death stand over men and none can escape them, they should go forward and win glory.
greek_mythology.explanation: Because death cannot be avoided, Sarpedon argues, it is better to live and die with honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same reasoning as the Kural: since there is no medicine against death, do not trade honour for survival.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close logic (inevitable death makes honour the better choice); paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The difficulty, my friends, is not in avoiding death, but in avoiding unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says the real danger is not death, which comes anyway, but doing wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says saving one's body is no remedy, while losing one's worth is the real loss.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close fit; Socrates speaks of unrighteousness rather than loss of dignity.

kurals.tamil:
மயிர்நீப்பின் வாழாக் கவரிமா அன்னார்
உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mayirneeppin vaazhaak kavarimaa annaar
Uyirneeppar maanam varin.
kurals.meaning: Like the yak said not to survive the loss of its hair, people of honour would give up life itself rather than live when their honour is taken from them.
kurals.elementary: An old story says the yak loves its long, beautiful hair so much it cannot live without it. This kural uses that story to say that some people treasure their good name the way the yak treasures its hair: nothing is worth losing it for.
kurals.university: The kavarimaa (கவரிமா) is the yak (Bos grunniens), whose tail-hair was prized for the chowrie or royal fly-whisk (chamara); popular Tamil usage later turned it into 'kavarimaan', a deer, though commentators identify it as the yak. The belief that it dies on losing its hair is poetic convention, not natural history; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as losing all its hair. Maanam varin (மானம் வரின்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as 'if honour is about to be destroyed'. The Parimelazhagar tradition sees here the culmination of the chapter: honour valued above life. This is classical heroic ethics and should be read historically, as a statement of honour's supreme worth, not as a recommendation to end one's life; several traditions compared below explicitly reject taking one's own life. Text identical on both sources; Pope: 'Like the wild ox that, of its tuft bereft, will pine away.'

hinduism.quote_or_event: Warned by his father Surya that Indra will come disguised as a Brahmin to ask for his divine armour and earrings, Karna still gives them away when asked, cutting them from his body, because he has vowed never to refuse a gift and will not break his word even to save his life.
hinduism.explanation: Karna gives up his protection, knowing it may cost him his life, rather than lose his honour as a giver.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's yak, Karna will not keep living at the price of what makes him who he is.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit on honour above life; he risks death rather than choosing it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection:”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews honours believers who refused release from torture rather than renounce their faith.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's honourable, they valued something above survival.
christianity._accuracy_note: Fits only the value-above-life element; Christianity honours enduring martyrdom, not choosing death, and does not permit self-killing.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly but only [in lawful] business by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves [or one another]. Indeed, Allah is to you ever Merciful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran forbids taking one's own life.
islam.tie_back: This is an honest counterpoint: Islam values honour but rejects the Kural's ideal of giving up life when honour is lost.
islam._accuracy_note: Contrast rather than parallel; included because no Islamic source endorses the Kural's point here.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud rules that for three sins, idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and murder, a person must let himself be killed rather than commit them: yehareg ve'al ya'avor, let him be killed and not transgress.
judaism.explanation: Jewish law names a few lines that must not be crossed even to save one's life.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets certain values above life itself, though the trigger is a forced sin, not loss of personal honour.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares 'value above life' but limits it to three sins; Judaism does not permit self-killing over dishonour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Path of Purification, Buddhaghosa tells the monk to guard his virtue like a hen guarding her eggs, or like a yak (camari) guarding its tail, or like a mother her only child, or a person their only eye.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist commentary uses the very same animal, the yak that guards its tail-hair at any cost, as the image of guarding one's moral purity.
buddhism.tie_back: The same yak image as the Kural, but applied to protecting virtue, not to giving up life.
buddhism.source: Buddhaghosa, Visuddhimagga I (on guarding virtue; tr. Bhikkhu Nanamoli, The Path of Purification)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking shared image of the yak; paraphrased from the commentary, and Buddhism does not endorse dying for honour.

jainism.quote_or_event: Amritachandra discusses sallekhana, the gradual, vowed giving up of food at the end of life, and argues that it is not suicide because it is undertaken without passion; by contrast, a person who ends their life under the sway of passions such as anger or wounded pride commits himsa against the self.
jainism.explanation: Jainism allows a calm, vowed death only in narrow conditions and treats dying out of injured pride as a form of violence.
jainism.tie_back: This is an honest contrast: Jain teaching would see a death prompted by lost honour (mana) as a passion to be overcome, not an ideal.
jainism.source: Amritachandra, Purusharthasiddhyupaya, verses on sallekhana (c. vv. 175-180; tr. Ajit Prasada)
jainism._accuracy_note: Doctrinal contrast, scored low; verse numbers given approximately and paraphrased without live verification of the translation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles' Ajax, the hero, shamed after his madness, tells his wife Tecmessa that a man of noble birth must either live with honour or die with honour, and then goes alone to the shore rather than live disgraced.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ajax holds that a noble person cannot go on living once his honour is gone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the tragic Greek counterpart of the Kural's yak: life is not worth keeping without honour.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close parallel to the honour-above-life ideal; the play presents it as tragedy, not as a model.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that to die in order to escape poverty, love or anything painful is not the mark of a brave man but of a coward, because it is running from trouble rather than facing it for a noble end.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, giving up life to flee suffering is not courage.
philosophy.tie_back: An honest counterweight to the Kural: classical philosophy questions dying to escape disgrace.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 3.7, 1116a12-15 (tr. W. D. Ross)

kurals.tamil:
இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார்
ஒளிதொழுது ஏத்தும் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilivarin vaazhaadha maanam udaiyaar
Olidhozhudhu eththum ulagu.
kurals.meaning: The world forever bows to and praises the glory of honourable people who would not go on living in disgrace.
kurals.elementary: People remember and admire heroes who never gave up doing what was right, even when it was very hard. This kural says the whole world keeps honouring such people long after they are gone.
kurals.university: Ilivu (இளிவு) is disgrace, humiliation; ilivarin vaazhaadha (இளிவரின் வாழாத) are those who 'do not live on when disgrace comes'. Oli (ஒளி), literally 'light', here means radiant fame, the glory that survives a person; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as pugazh (புகழ்) or pugazh vadivu (the form of one's fame). Thozhudhu eththum (தொழுது ஏத்தும்) is the language of worship: folding hands and praising. The chapter closes where Tamil heroic ethics often closes, with lasting fame as the reward of honour. Read today, its lasting point is that the world reveres those who keep their integrity at great cost. Pope: 'Who, when dishonour comes, refuse to live, their honoured memory / Will live in worship and applause of all the world for aye!' Text identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra keeps his word to the sage Vishvamitra though it costs him his kingdom, his wife and son, and his freedom, working at last as a servant at a cremation ground; the gods finally restore him, and his name became the Indian byword for truthfulness.
hinduism.explanation: Harishchandra suffers every loss rather than break his word, and is remembered and revered for it.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural's honourable person whose glory the world still praises.
hinduism.source: Markandeya Purana, chapters 7-8 (tr. F. E. Pargiter)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong fit on lasting veneration for honour kept at great cost; he endures rather than dies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews says Abel's faithfulness still speaks long after his death.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural too says the glory of the honourable outlives them.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches lasting witness after death; the cause is faith, not honour.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We gave them of Our mercy, and We made for them a mention [i.e., reputation] of high honor.”
islam.explanation: Speaking of Abraham and his descendants, the Quran says God gave them an honoured name among later generations.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises enduring renown to those who held to what was right.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit on lasting honourable reputation; given by God rather than by the world's praise.

judaism.quote_or_event: The aged scribe Eleazar, ordered to eat pork, refuses even to pretend, saying it does not befit his years to deceive the young; he goes to his death, and the book says he left his death as an example of noble courage and a memorial of virtue for the young and for the whole nation.
judaism.explanation: Eleazar chooses death over a disgraceful pretence and is remembered as a model.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural's scene: one who would not live in disgrace becomes a lasting memorial honoured by his people.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative; 2 Maccabees is a Hellenistic Jewish work outside the Hebrew Tanakh, and the cause is fidelity to the law.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not the sweet smell of flowers, not even the fragrance of sandal, tagara, or jasmine blows against the wind. But the fragrance of the virtuous blows against the wind. Truly the virtuous man pervades all directions with the fragrance of his virtue.”
buddhism.explanation: The good name of the virtuous spreads everywhere, even against the wind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says the glory of the honourable spreads through the world.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit on far-spreading fame of the virtuous; nothing about refusing to live in disgrace.

jainism.quote_or_event: The opening verse of the Dasavaikalika Sutra calls dharma the highest good, names non-violence, self-control and austerity as its essence, and says that even the gods bow down to one whose mind is always set on dharma.
jainism.explanation: In Jainism it is the person firm in dharma who receives the homage of gods and humans.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's world bows to the honourable; the Jain verse says even the gods bow to the steadfast in dharma.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 1.1 (as Saman Suttam v. 82, tr. T. K. Tukol and K. K. Dixit)
jainism._accuracy_note: Matches the image of reverence; the object is dharma and self-control, not worldly honour. Paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells the embassy that his mother foretold two fates: if he stays and fights at Troy he will not return home but his glory (kleos) will never perish; if he goes home he will live long without fame.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles weighs a long life against undying glory.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural promises the same reward, lasting worldly praise, to those who put honour before life.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong fit on imperishable fame as honour's reward; Achilles' motives are mixed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his funeral oration, Pericles says that the fallen gave their lives and in return won praise that never grows old, and that the whole earth is the tomb of famous men, whose memory lives on far from home.
philosophy.explanation: Pericles says those who died rather than accept defeat are remembered everywhere.
philosophy.tie_back: Close to the Kural's world that worships the glory of the honourable.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.43 (tr. Richard Crawley)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong fit on enduring public honour; a civic speech, paraphrased.
